power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We tested N = 405 participants (52.1% female), aged 18-80 (MAge = 44.8) from Prolific in a preregistered study: https://osf.io/2u3wc/overview?view_only=af15f6d30a124aa0ac716212de0b79e0. Participants were compensated $2.85 for participating in a 17-min survey. We initially recruited 416 participants, but 11 were excluded for failing our inclusion criteria. Sample size was determined using a statistical power simulation with data from Study 4 which found we would have 100% power (95% CI: 99.63, 100%) to detect an effect of emotion condition with N = 400 given the effect size observed in Study 4 for the intent measure.
table.effect_size_metric_other: effect size observed in Study 4 for the intent measure

table.text: We sampled N = 193 participants (64.8% female), aged 18-75 (MAge = 38.2) from Prolific. Participants were compensated $1.40 for participating in a 7-min survey. We conducted an a priori power calculation using the semPower package (Moshagen & Bader, 2024) in R to determine the number of participants needed to reject a model based on a root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) of 0.05, 169 degrees of freedom, 90% power, and an alpha of 0.05 (Jobst et al., 2023). The analysis suggested a minimum sample of 148 observations. We consequently oversampled to account for potential attrition due to failed attention checks or incomplete submissions.

Although we preregistered LMEMs controlling for the random intercepts of participant and vignette identity, after data analysis we determined that these models were underpowered for our central comparison between cringe and vicarious embarrassment. Because the two scenario conditions used different vignettes (five each), treating vignettes as a random factor meant that the condition effect is estimated from just 10 vignettes rather than from 405 participants (Judd et al., 2012). These tests are therefore very conservative and are powered to detect only large differences between the two sets of vignettes (approximately d ≥ 2.0; Westfall et al., 2014). We therefore deviated from our preregistration: We report LMEMs with a random intercept for participant ID here and report the preregistered models with crossed random intercepts for participant and vignette in the supplement (see Study 5 -Results). Because the two sets of models address different questions-whether participants distinguished our particular cringe and vicarious embarrassment vignettes, and whether these differences generalize to cringe and vicarious embarrassment scenarios more broadly-we discuss the results of both in the Study 5 Discussion.

table.title: Cringe scale - Study 2
table.research_questions:
Our objectives in this study are three-fold:
1. Validate the psychometric properties of our cringe sensitivity scale.
2. Confirm that our selected cringe stimuli are indeed perceived as cringey.
3. Determine whether cringe sensitivity scale score is associated with individual cringe assessments.

H1: A confirmatory factor analysis will find evidence for our 2-factor scale of trait-cringe.
To address objective 1, we will conduct a Confirmatory Factor Analysis of our 20-item cringe sensitivity scale specifying the following factor structure: items 1-12 load onto factor 1 (general cringe) and items 13-20 will load onto factor 2 (fakeness-inauthenticity). We hypothesize that our model-implied covariance matrix Σ(θ) will be equal to the observed covariance matrix Σ. The alternative hypothesis is that the model implied covariance matrix is not equal to the observed covariance matrix. In this case, we do not want to reject the null hypothesis.

H0 : Σ(θ) = Σ
H1 : Σ(θ)̸ = Σ

Additionally, we expect that our two correlated factor model will fit the data better than a second- order two-factor model

H2: Cringe stimuli will be rated as more cringey than the neutral stimuli.
To address objective 2, we will conduct a Randomized Controlled Trial in which treatment group participants will receive cringey stimuli, and control group participants will receive neutral stimuli. We hypothesize that our cringe manipulation will result in a statistically significant average treatment effect such that stimuli in our cringe condition will be rated as higher in cringe than the neutral condition at α = 0.05.

H3: Scores on our trait-cringe scale will predict cringe perceptions in the cringe vignettes and videos.  
To address objective 3, we will pool all participants and estimate an association between cringe sensitivity scale scores and cringe assessments. We hypothesize a statistically significant association between trait cringe sensitivity and cringe assessments at α = 0.05.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
table.study_design_overview:
Using the online platform Prolific, we will randomly assign participants to the treatment or control group in a between-subject design. Both groups will self-report their agreement with items in our cringe scale. After this, they will read a series of short vignettes, longer vignettes, and watch several short videos. The treatment group’s stimuli are intended to be cringey, while the control group’s stimuli are intended to be non-cringey. Specific details about the stimuli will be presented in the Appendix. 

The order in which stimuli will be presented will be randomized within each condition. Our intended sample size is n = 300, with n = 150 assigned to each group. We will deliberately oversample by 10 to account for attrition and failed attention checks. This study is single-blind, as the participants will not know to which condition they were assigned, but we will know this information.
table.randomization: Participants will be randomly assigned to either a cringe or neutral experimental condition in a between-subject design. Participants will receive all three types of cringe stimuli (short scenarios, long vignettes, and videos) in a randomized order within-subjects.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: We will collect a sample of participants from Prolific crowdsourcing platform. All participants will be English speakers from the U.S. Participants will receive approximately $2.10 in compensation for completing a 10-12-minute Qualtrics survey.
table.sample_size: We will collect a sample of N = 310.
table.sample_size_rationale: Sample size was based on past work using confirmatory factor analysis for scale development. These numbers are approximate due to our recruitment via Prolific and the possibility that we will need to top up our sample due to exclusions (see Data exclusion). Our top up procedure (see Other) will ensure that we have a minimum of 150 participants per condition.
table.stopping_rule: We will stop data collection when we reach at least N = 150 per condition.
table.manipulated_variables: Participants will be assigned to one of two experimental conditions: neutral (control) or treatment (cringe).
table.measured_variables:
Cringe sensitivity scale Items:
The following items will be evaluated on an agreement scale ranging from “1 - Completely Disagree” to
“7-Completely Agree”. The variable names are in parentheses and emboldened.
1. I fidget or tense up when I watch something embarrassing happen. (physical1)
2. I feel my cheeks heat up when something embarrassing happens to others around me. (physical2)
3. I get nervous when I see someone else in an awkward or uncomfortable situation. (physical3)
4. I get a tight feeling in my chest when I witness embarrassing moments. (physical4)
5. I feel embarrassed if someone makes a mistake in front of a crowd. (ve1)
6. I get embarrassed by others’ public humiliation. (ve2)
7. I tend to anticipate and worry about others making social mistakes. (ve3)
8. If I witness someone making a social blunder, I feel just as embarrassed as if it happened to me. (ve4)
9. I feel physically uncomfortable when someone acts out of place or inappropriately in social situations. (norm1)
10. When people dress or behave in ways that are inappropriate for the occasion, it makes me feel uncomfortable. (norm2)
11. I get anxious when I’m around people who don’t seem to understand or care about social rules. (norm3)
12. I feel stressed when someone behaves in a socially awkward or out-of-sync way. (norm4)
13. I feel embarrassed for people who try too hard to appear cooler or more interesting than they actually are. (fake1)
14. I feel awkward when I see people putting on a fake persona in social situations. (fake2)
15. I feel uncomfortable watching people try too hard to impress others. (fake3)
16. When someone is being disingenuous in a conversation, I find it difficult to watch or listen. (fake4)
17. Seeing someone imitate a trend or behavior just to be part of the crowd makes me uncomfortable. (fake5)
18. It’s embarrassing when someone’s confidence comes across as staged or forced. (fake6)
19. It’s embarrassing watching someone seek social approval or validation. (fake7)
20. I feel uneasy when someone’s behavior feels rehearsed or overly polished. (fake8)

Cringe Assessment:
In response to the cringe stimuli (i.e. short scenarios, long vignettes, videos), participants will be given the following direction: “Please rate the extent to which you perceive each scenario/video as ‘cringe’.” They will then use a 100 point sliding scale with text anchors at each pole reading “Not cringe at all” to “Extremely cringe.”

Demographics:

table.title: Cringe scale - Study 3
table.research_questions:
Our objectives in this study are three-fold:
1. Validate the psychometric properties of the Cringe Sensitivity Scale.
2. Determine whether cringe is a distinct latent construct from vicarious embarrassment.
3. Determine whether cringe is associated with behavioral outcomes and intentions.

Hypothesis 1. A Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) will provide supportive evidence for our 2-
factor Cringe Scale. Specifically, we expect that items 1-12 from the Cringe Scale will load on to factor η1 (general cringe), and that items 13-20 will load on to factor η2 (fakeness/inauthenticity). Further, we hypothesize that our model-implied covariance matrix Σ(Θ) will be equal to the observed covariance matrix Σ. We denote this as:
H0 : Σ(θ) = Σ
H1 : Σ(θ) ≠Σ
In this case, we do not want to reject the null hypothesis.

Hypothesis 2. Discriminant validity testing will provide evidence in support for our hypothesis that cringe and vicarious embarrassment are distinct constructs.

Hypothesis 3a. Cringe scale scores will be significantly associated with donation and
intention behaviors such that higher cringe scores will be associated with lower donations and intentions of engaging in the relevant behavior.

Hypothesis 3b. The video treatment condition (cringe, neutral) will be significantly associated with donation and intention behaviors such that donations and behavioral intentions will be lower in the cringe condition than the control condition.

table.title: Cringe scale - Study 5
table.research_questions:
Research question 1: Is cringe perceived differently than vicarious embarrassment? 
1. Participants will rate the cringe vignettes as more cringe than the vicarious embarrassment vignettes and will rate the vicariously embarrassing vignettes as more vicariously embarrassing than the cringe vignettes.
2. Participants will rate the cringe vignettes as lower in empathy, norm awareness, prosocial motivation, and attention seeking, but higher in norm violation, punishment, moral wrongness, and intent, than the vicarious embarrassment vignettes. 
3. The intentional vignettes will be perceived as more cringe and less vicariously embarrassing than the unintentional vignettes.

Research question 2: Does cringe scale score predict vignette ratings of norm awareness, norm violation, and punishment?
4. Participants' scores on the cringe scale will positively predict ratings of norm violation and punishment expectations.
5. Cringe scale scores will positively predict appropriateness ratings of the punishment responses. 

Research question 3: What is the role of intent in the relationship between cringe perceptions, vicarious embarrassment, moral judgments, normative violation perceptions, punishment, and prosocial motivation? 
6. Intent will mediate the relationship between emotion condition (cringe, vicarious embarrassment) and moral wrongness judgements and norm violation perceptions.
7. Moral wrongness judgements and norm violation perceptions will mediate the relationship between intent and prosocial motivation and punishment ratings. 
8. The global model with intent will fit the data better than the model without intent. 

Research question 4: Do norm violation perceptions underlie the effect of cringe sensitivity on cringe perceptions?
9. Perceptions of norm violations will mediate the effect of cringe sensitivity on cringe perceptions.

Research question 5: How do reputational concerns influence the expression of cringe? 
10. Reported perceptions of cringe will be higher when experienced publicly in front of others than when experienced privately.

In the event that this threshold is ≥ 3%, then we will perform a sensitivity analysis using multiple imputations through chained equations with the number of imputations M equal to max(5, 100f), where f is the proportion of observations with any missing data (following Harrell, 2025).

table.title: Cringe scale - Study 5
table.research_questions:
Research question 1: Is cringe perceived differently than vicarious embarrassment? 
1. Participants will rate the cringe vignettes as more cringe than the vicarious embarrassment vignettes and will rate the vicariously embarrassing vignettes as more vicariously embarrassing than the cringe vignettes.
2. Participants will rate the cringe vignettes as lower in empathy, norm awareness, prosocial motivation, and attention seeking, but higher in norm violation, punishment, moral wrongness, and intent, than the vicarious embarrassment vignettes. 
3. The intentional vignettes will be perceived as more cringe and less vicariously embarrassing than the unintentional vignettes.

Research question 2: Does cringe scale score predict vignette ratings of norm awareness, norm violation, and punishment?
4. Participants' scores on the cringe scale will positively predict ratings of norm violation and punishment expectations.
5. Cringe scale scores will positively predict appropriateness ratings of the punishment responses. 

Research question 3: What is the role of intent in the relationship between cringe perceptions, vicarious embarrassment, moral judgments, normative violation perceptions, punishment, and prosocial motivation? 
6. Intent will mediate the relationship between emotion condition (cringe, vicarious embarrassment) and moral wrongness judgements and norm violation perceptions.
7. Moral wrongness judgements and norm violation perceptions will mediate the relationship between intent and prosocial motivation and punishment ratings. 
8. The global model with intent will fit the data better than the model without intent. 

Research question 4: Do norm violation perceptions underlie the effect of cringe sensitivity on cringe perceptions?
9. Perceptions of norm violations will mediate the effect of cringe sensitivity on cringe perceptions.

Research question 5: How do reputational concerns influence the expression of cringe? 
10. Reported perceptions of cringe will be higher when experienced publicly in front of others than when experienced privately.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
table.study_design_overview: Participants will be randomly assigned to either a cringe or vicarious embarrassment condition between-subjects, an intent or accidental behavior condition between-subjects, and a public or private reputation condition between-subjects. Participants will see five cringe or vicariously embarrassing scenarios depending on their experimental condition and will answer a series of measures for each (see Behavior dimension ratings in Measures). After participants receive those five behaviors, they will generate their own example of cringe or vicarious embarrassment (depending on their condition assignment) and answer the same set of measures. Participants will then see five more behaviors that vary in their intent (intentional or accidental) and will rate their cringe and vicarious embarrassment perceptions for each. Next, participants will receive the reputation manipulation in which they will read three scenarios depicting social transgressions that vary in whether they occur publicly or privately. Participants will report their cringe perceptions for each scenario. Lastly, participants will answer several demographic questions, following which the study will end.
table.randomization: Participants will be randomly assigned to either the Cringe or Vicarious Embarrassment stimuli condition, intent or accidental condition, public or private reputation condition, all between-subjects. Randomization will be performed by a Randomizer program on the Qualtrics platform. The behavior dimension measures will be presented in a randomized order with the exception of the prosocial motivation measure which always came at the end of the question block.

table.data_collection_procedures: We will collect a sample of participants from the Prolific crowdsourcing platform.
table.sample_size: We will collect a sample of N = 415 to ensure we have at least N = 200 per condition post exclusions (see Data exclusions below).
table.sample_size_rationale:
Sample size was determined using a statistical power simulation with data from Study 4 which found we would have 100% power (95% CI: 99.63, 100%) to detect an effect of emotion condition with N = 400 given the effect size observed in Study 4 for the intent measure. 
These numbers are approximate due to our recruitment via Prolific and the possibility that we will need to top up our sample due to exclusions (see Data exclusion). Our top up procedure (see Other) will ensure that we have a minimum of 200 per condition.
table.stopping_rule: We will stop data collection when we reach N = 200 per condition.
table.manipulated_variables: Participants will be assigned to one of two emotion stimuli conditions (Cringe, Vicarious Embarrassment), one of two intent conditions (intentional, accidental), and one of two reputation conditions (private, public).
table.measured_variables:
Vignette intensity ratings: Self-report ratings on 100pt sliding scale measuring the following constructs.
Cringe: How much cringe would you feel observing this situation?
Vicarious embarrassment: How much second-hand embarrassment would you feel observing this situation?

Behavior dimension ratings: Delf-report ratings on 100pt sliding scale measuring the following constructs.
Affective empathy: To what extent do you feel the same emotions that someone in this scenario is feeling?
Moral wrongness: How morally wrong is the act described in this scenario?
Norm awareness: Do you think the person in this scenario was aware that they violated a social norm or acted inappropriately? 
Norm violation: To what extent do you think that the person in this scenario violated a social norm or social convention?
Attention seeking: To what extent do you think that the person in this scenario was trying to get attention or impress others?
Intent: How intentional was the behavior in this scenario?
Punishment: In your opinion, should the person in this scenario be punished by others?
Punish response: Please rate how appropriate each of the following behaviors would be in response to the person’s actions described in this scenario. [nothing, gossip, social exclusion, verbal confrontation]
Prosocial motivation: Imagine that you later saw the person in this scenario drop a handful of change. How likely would you be to stop and help them pick it up?

The Cringe Scale: A 20-item Cringe Scale with all item responses presented on a 7-point-Likert scale anchored from “1-Complete disagree” to “7-Completely agree.”
1. I fidget or tense up when I watch something embarrassing happen.
2. I feel my cheeks heat up when something embarrassing happens to others around me.
3. I get nervous when I see someone else in an awkward or uncomfortable situation.
4. I get a tight feeling in my chest when I witness embarrassing moments.
5. I feel embarrassed if someone makes a mistake in front of a crowd.
6. I get embarrassed by others’ public humiliation.
7. I tend to anticipate and worry about others making social mistakes.
8 If I witness someone making a social blunder, I feel just as embarrassed as if it happened to me.
9. I feel physically uncomfortable when someone acts out of place or inappropriately in social situations.
10. When people dress or behave in ways that are inappropriate for the occasion, it makes me feel uncomfortable.
11. I get anxious when I’m around people who don’t seem to understand or care about social rules.
12. I feel stressed when someone behaves in a socially awkward or out-of-sync way.
13. I feel embarrassed for people who try too hard to appear cooler or more interesting than they actually are.
14. I feel awkward when I see people putting on a fake persona in social situations.
15. I feel uncomfortable watching people try too hard to impress others.
16. When someone is being disingenuous in a conversation, I find it difficult to watch or listen.
17. Seeing someone imitate a trend or behavior just to be part of the crowd makes me uncomfortable.
18. It’s embarrassing when someone’s confidence comes across as staged or forced.
19. It’s embarrassing watching someone seek social approval or validation.
20. I feel uneasy when someone’s behavior feels rehearsed or overly polished.

stat_check.title: StatCheck
stat_check.summary_text: We detected no errors in t-tests or F-tests.

table.text: However, when testing whether the Cringe Scale and VES differed in their ability to predict cringe assessments by comparing regression coefficients using seemingly unrelated regression (SUR), we found that a Theil's F test indicated no significant difference between the coefficients (F(1, 590) = 0.10, p = .75), suggesting both scales have equivalent predictive validity for cringe assessments.

stat_check.report: We detected no errors in t-tests or F-tests.

table.formatted: Simple slope analyses found that Cringe Scale score was negatively associated with the appropriateness of not punishing (B = -3.53, SE = 0.88, p < .001)-indicating that individuals higher in trait cringe sensitivity viewed non-punishment as less appropriate-and positively predicted appropriateness ratings of gossip (B = 2.23, SE = 0.88, p = .016), social exclusion (B = 2.33, SE = 0.88, p = .016), and verbal confrontation (B = 3.33, SE = 0.88, p < .001), suggesting that individuals high in trait cringe are more likely to approve of sanctioning norm violators.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. #### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 9 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (9). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 617 columns across 9 data files.
#### Issues Identified

49 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

**What this does not cover.** Only 8 of 9 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 6 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  6 of 6 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  17 installable dependencies detected.
- 4544 statistics stored from the extracted output; 91 of 121 reported tests matched (75.2%).

live_data_statements: We sampled N = 193 participants (64.8% female), aged 18-75 (MAge = 38.2) from Prolific.
Participants were compensated $1.40 for participating in a 7-min survey.
Participants provided informed consent and were given instructions for the task.

We sampled N = 310 participants (49.7% female), aged 19-85 (MAge = 45.9) from Prolific in a preregistered study with a representative sample from the US population: https://osf.io/ymzqc/overview?view_only=b9463362065e4965b0edd18a728fba9e.

After answering the Cringe Scale items, participants were randomly assigned between-subjects to a cringe or neutral scenario condition in which they received 10 short scenarios, 4 vignettes, and 4 short (around 1 minute) videos corresponding to their experimental condition.
We sampled N = 307 participants (51.8% female), aged 19-72 (MAge = 38.74) from Prolific in a preregistered study: https://osf.io/2q73k/overview?view_only=4ecf65adc28d47ac9ea670175c3bc12b.
Participants were compensated $2.50 for participating in a 15-min survey.
To that end, participants completed our 20-item Cringe Scale from Study 2 as well as the 8-item Vicarious Embarrassment scale (VES; Uysal et al., 2014), which they received in a random order.
Participants were then randomly assigned to either a cringe or neutral emotion condition between-subjects and saw five videos corresponding to their assigned condition in a fixed order.
Participants completed an incentivized donation task (i.e., a dictator game with the nonprofit as the recipient) after watching each of the nonprofit videos.
We tested N = 200 participants (53.0% female), aged 21-77 (MAge = 41.2) from Prolific.
Participants were compensated $1.85 for participating in a 10-min survey.
No participants were excluded from analysis.
Participants were assigned to either a cringe or vicarious embarrassment scenario condition between-subjects.

Participants were provided with a short, colloquial definition of their condition's emotion (see Study 4 -Supplementary Materials for definition text) and were asked to generate three short example scenarios that best capture that emotion.
Doing so allowed us to capture lay perceptions of these two emotions and mitigate concerns that participants were anchoring their responses to the experimenter-provided definitions from Study 4.
We tested N = 405 participants (52.1% female), aged 18-80 (MAge = 44.8) from Prolific in a preregistered study: https://osf.io/2u3wc/overview?view_only=af15f6d30a124aa0ac716212de0b79e0.
Participants were compensated $2.85 for participating in a 17-min survey.

Participants were randomly assigned to either a cringe or vicarious embarrassment condition, an intentional or accidental vignette condition, and to a public or private reputation condition, all between-subjects.
Participants were then asked to generate their own example scenario of cringe or vicarious embarrassment, depending on their condition assignment, and rated it on the same nine measures.
After the reputation vignettes, participants completed our 20item Cringe Scale.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 6 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:6, File = c("cringe.s1_osf_top.Rmd", 
"cringe.s2_osf_top.Rmd", "cringe.s3_osf_top.Rmd", "cringe.s4_osf_top.Rmd", 
"cringe.s5_osf_top.Rmd", "cringe.combined_osf_top.Rmd"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"—", "—", "—", "—", "—"), Basis = c("numeric", "numeric", 
"numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "none")), row.names = c(NA, 
-6L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**9 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `cringe.s3.wide_osf.csv` to `../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe.s3.wide_osf.csv` (in cringe.s3_osf_top.Rmd); `cringe.s5_osf.csv` to `../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe.s5_osf.csv` (in cringe.s5_osf_top.Rmd); `cringe.s5.wide_osf.csv` to `../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe.s5.wide_osf.csv` (in cringe.s5_osf_top.Rmd); `cringe_combined.CFA_wide.csv` to `../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe_combined.CFA_wide.csv` (in cringe.combined_osf_top.Rmd); `cringe_combined.csv` to `../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe_combined.csv` (in cringe.combined_osf_top.Rmd); `cringe.s3.wide_osf.csv` to `../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe.s3.wide_osf.csv` (in cringe.combined_osf_top.Rmd); `cringe.s2_osf.csv` to `../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe.s2_osf.csv` (in cringe.s2_osf_top.Rmd); `cringe.s4_osf.csv` to `../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe.s4_osf.csv` (in cringe.s4_osf_top.Rmd); `cringe.s1_osf.csv` to `../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe.s1_osf.csv` (in cringe.s1_osf_top.Rmd). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. **1 data path was built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 6 scripts: 6 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

text.text: Draft version 2.0, 11/4/26.
This paper has not been peer reviewed.
Cringe-a term used to describe situations perceived as intensely embarrassing, awkward, or just generally discomforting-is ubiquitous in modern culture and social life.

It is used without elaboration on the pages of the New York Times (McNicholas, 2025), graduation commencement speeches (Swift, 2022), social media platforms (Reddit, 2026), and throughout popular media.
text.formatted: It is used without elaboration on the pages of the New York Times <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(McNicholas, 2025)</ref>, graduation commencement speeches <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Swift, 2022)</ref>, social media platforms <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Reddit, 2026)</ref>, and throughout popular media.

text.text: Yet, despite its growing usage and ubiquity in everyday life, we currently understand very little about cringe as an emotional state or trait.

Although cringe is commonly used as an evaluative label for socially inept behavior ("he is so cringe"), it is more than a descriptor-it exhibits features that most emotion theorists view as constituting emotion, such as reliable antecedents, appraisal processes, and action tendencies (Ekman, 1992 (Ekman, , 2016;; Keltner & Buswell, 1997).
text.formatted: Although cringe is commonly used as an evaluative label for socially inept behavior ("he is so cringe"), it is more than a descriptor-it exhibits features that most emotion theorists view as constituting emotion, such as reliable antecedents, appraisal processes, and action tendencies <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Ekman, 1992</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Ekman, , 2016;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Keltner & Buswell, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Nor is cringe a new concept; while its use has surged in recent years, the underlying affective state we call cringe likely predates the contemporary usage of the term (e.g., cringeworthy dates back to the 1970s; Oxford English Dictionary, n.d.).
Cringe warrants greater scientific attention because of its growing role in social life.

It has become a monetized media commodity (Mayer et al., 2021), shapes how audiences respond to persuasive messaging (Escoe et al., 2025), and is frequently used to label and shame non-conforming individuals, particularly on social media.
text.formatted: It has become a monetized media commodity <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Mayer et al., 2021)</ref>, shapes how audiences respond to persuasive messaging <ref type="bibr">(Escoe et al., 2025)</ref>, and is frequently used to label and shame non-conforming individuals, particularly on social media.

text.text: Cringe may also contribute to social-developmental difficulties among young people: the fear of being labeled cringe, and the shame associated with it, has been linked to social anxiety (Mzizi, 2025; The Learning Network, 2025), and in a recent Yahoo/YouGov poll, more than half of adult Gen Z respondents reported that fear of seeming cringe had kept them from expressing themselves online and from opening up emotionally (Weekman, 2026).
text.formatted: Cringe may also contribute to social-developmental difficulties among young people: the fear of being labeled cringe, and the shame associated with it, has been linked to social anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Mzizi, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">The Learning Network, 2025)</ref>, and in a recent Yahoo/YouGov poll, more than half of adult Gen Z respondents reported that fear of seeming cringe had kept them from expressing themselves online and from opening up emotionally <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Weekman, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: While academic work on cringe remains sparse, the way the term is colloquially used suggests that it is likely a social emotion, given its close connection to social interaction and expectations, and thus differs from basic emotions such as fear, sadness, or disgust (Ekman, 1992; Izard, 1992).
text.formatted: While academic work on cringe remains sparse, the way the term is colloquially used suggests that it is likely a social emotion, given its close connection to social interaction and expectations, and thus differs from basic emotions such as fear, sadness, or disgust <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Ekman, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Izard, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, cringe is perhaps best conceptualized as a "self-conscious emotion"-a category of social emotions that relate to our sense of self, arise from our awareness of how others perceive us, and are highly sensitive to social context in their expression and intensity (Hareli & Parkinson, 2008; Thomas et al., 2018; Tracy et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Moreover, cringe is perhaps best conceptualized as a "self-conscious emotion"-a category of social emotions that relate to our sense of self, arise from our awareness of how others perceive us, and are highly sensitive to social context in their expression and intensity <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hareli & Parkinson, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Thomas et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Tracy et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Self-conscious emotions such as shame, embarrassment, and guilt play important roles in maintaining and repairing social relationships following social transgressions that damage the transgressor's reputation, as well as motivating individuals to behave in moral, socially appropriate ways (Thomas et al., 2018; Tracy et al., 2009; Tracy & Robins, 2004).
text.formatted: Self-conscious emotions such as shame, embarrassment, and guilt play important roles in maintaining and repairing social relationships following social transgressions that damage the transgressor's reputation, as well as motivating individuals to behave in moral, socially appropriate ways <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Thomas et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Tracy et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Tracy & Robins, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: This emphasis on adaptive functions underlies the form-function approach to studying emotions which holds that an emotion's form (e.g., its features and characteristics) is shaped by its function, the adaptive problem it evolved to solve (Cosmides & Tooby, 2000; Nesse, 1990; Sznycer, 2019).
text.formatted: This emphasis on adaptive functions underlies the form-function approach to studying emotions which holds that an emotion's form (e.g., its features and characteristics) is shaped by its function, the adaptive problem it evolved to solve <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cosmides & Tooby, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Nesse, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Sznycer, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In this view, self-conscious emotions are adaptations for navigating social life: following a transgression, they serve a "recalibration" function that bolsters others' evaluations of the transgressor and maintains cooperative relationships (Sznycer, 2019; Sznycer et al., 2021; Thomas et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In this view, self-conscious emotions are adaptations for navigating social life: following a transgression, they serve a "recalibration" function that bolsters others' evaluations of the transgressor and maintains cooperative relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Sznycer, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Sznycer et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Thomas et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: We draw on the form-function approach here to conceptualize cringe in relation to other self-conscious social emotions. 1Specifically, we propose that cringe may have a function in human social cognition, akin to but distinct from embarrassment or shame, in underlying social norm conformity and enforcement.
text.formatted: We draw on the form-function approach here to conceptualize cringe in relation to other self-conscious social emotions. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">1</ref>Specifically, we propose that cringe may have a function in human social cognition, akin to but distinct from embarrassment or shame, in underlying social norm conformity and enforcement.

text.text: Social norms are the tacit, unwritten rules that govern and constrain human behavior (Bicchieri, 2016; Legros & Cislaghi, 2020) and play a crucial role in underlying collective action and cooperation in groups (Fehr & Fischbacher, 2004; Ostrom, 2000).
text.formatted: Social norms are the tacit, unwritten rules that govern and constrain human behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bicchieri, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Legros & Cislaghi, 2020)</ref> and play a crucial role in underlying collective action and cooperation in groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Fehr & Fischbacher, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Ostrom, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Recent work finds that norm cognition and enforcement are proximately motivated by social emotions such as shame and embarrassment (Packard & Schultz, 2023; Schaumberg & Skowronek, 2022; Thomas et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Recent work finds that norm cognition and enforcement are proximately motivated by social emotions such as shame and embarrassment <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Packard & Schultz, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Schaumberg & Skowronek, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Thomas et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: For example, a growing literature demonstrates the importance of righteous anger and moral outrage in underlying norm enforcement-the anger we feel witnessing a freerider violate fairness norms motivates us to punish them, even when personally costly (Ginther et al., 2022; Jordan & Rand, 2020).

text.text: We hypothesize that, like moral outrage, cringe may serve an important function underlying norm compliance and enforcement-but unlike outrage, does so specifically for conventional norm violations (e.g., how we dress, behave in public, etc.
Rakoczy & Schmidt, 2013), rather than more serious moral violations.

text.text: Cringe is closely related to vicarious embarrassment (or secondhand embarrassment), the feeling of embarrassment derived from witnessing someone else embarrass themselves (Krach et al., 2011; Uysal et al., 2014; Ziegler et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Cringe is closely related to vicarious embarrassment (or secondhand embarrassment), the feeling of embarrassment derived from witnessing someone else embarrass themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Krach et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Uysal et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Ziegler et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Cringe, like vicarious embarrassment, is best conceptualized as a "secondhand emotion" felt vicariously through others when witnessing their transgression (regardless of whether the target is outwardly embarrassed or not).

Moreover, both cringe and vicarious embarrassment are experienced in response to witnessing faux pas, social ineptitude, or low-stakes norm violations, and both can elicit unconscious physiological and behavioral responses such as blushing or gaze avoidance (Thorstenson et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Moreover, both cringe and vicarious embarrassment are experienced in response to witnessing faux pas, social ineptitude, or low-stakes norm violations, and both can elicit unconscious physiological and behavioral responses such as blushing or gaze avoidance <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Thorstenson et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Lastly, cringe and vicarious embarrassment are both generally associated with a sense of discomfort and displeasure from witnessing a transgression, though somewhat paradoxically both can also be humorous, as demonstrated by the popularity of "cringe comedy" (Mayer et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Lastly, cringe and vicarious embarrassment are both generally associated with a sense of discomfort and displeasure from witnessing a transgression, though somewhat paradoxically both can also be humorous, as demonstrated by the popularity of "cringe comedy" <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Mayer et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Like most social emotions, including vicarious embarrassment, we propose that cringe can be measured as both a temporary fleeting state and as a stable dispositional trait.

We define state cringe as a transient, affective response to a specific perceived norm-violating situation or behavior, and cringe perceptions as evaluations of an individual or situation as state cringeinducing.
We define trait cringe as a stable individual difference in the tendency to react with feelings of awkwardness, unpleasantness, or avoidance in response to others' norm violations.

Consequently, we predict that there will be inter-individual differences in trait cringe sensitivity such that some individuals have a greater tendency to perceive and experience cringe compared to others.

Moreover, as with many emotions, state and trait cringe are likely associated (O'Malley & Gillette, 1984), such that high trait cringe is related to stronger feelings of temporary state cringe and perceptions of others as cringeworthy.
text.formatted: Moreover, as with many emotions, state and trait cringe are likely associated <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(O'Malley & Gillette, 1984)</ref>, such that high trait cringe is related to stronger feelings of temporary state cringe and perceptions of others as cringeworthy.

text.text: Despite their similarities, there are several important differences between vicarious embarrassment and cringe which suggest they may not be entirely overlapping constructs.

While vicarious embarrassment is elicited by observing normative transgressions, general ineptitude, or maladroitness, cringe is likely felt almost exclusively when witnessing normative transgressions.
Another potential key distinction between cringe and vicarious embarrassment concerns the perceived motivation of the transgressor-that is, why they transgressed.
Specifically, transgressors who elicit cringe may differ from those that elicit vicarious embarrassment in two key respects.

First, while vicarious embarrassment is often the result of unintentional actions (e.g., tripping in front of an attractive person, calling your teacher or boss "mom"), cringe is more likely to be elicited in response to intentional actions (e.g., trying to use slang to appear hip, wearing white to a wedding when you are not the bride).

Second, while embarrassment is associated with feelings of empathy, sympathy, or pity for the embarrassing individual (Krach et al., 2011; Miller, 1987; Stocks et al., 2011), the same is not true for cringe.
text.formatted: Second, while embarrassment is associated with feelings of empathy, sympathy, or pity for the embarrassing individual <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Krach et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Miller, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Stocks et al., 2011)</ref>, the same is not true for cringe.

text.text: We propose that when people experience cringe, they are relatively less inclined to empathize with or help the transgressor and more motivated to distance themselves from them (whether physically or reputationally).

In one of the only empirical studies of cringe, Escoe et al. (2025) defined cringe as a form of vicarious embarrassment in which an actor makes an awkward attempt at forming a positive impression in a way that is inexcusable.
Excusability refers to the observer's appraisal of the actor's transgression as forgivable because they are able to take the actor's perspective and understand why they transgressed.
In this view, cringe arises when observers fail to take the actor's perspective, resulting in negative attitudes and reduced compassion toward the transgressor.

Escoe et al. distinguish cringe from empathetic embarrassment, which occurs when the transgression is excusable and is consequently associated with more positive attitudes and greater compassion toward the transgressor.

In this account, sharing cringe content is motivated by downward social comparison that boosts perceptions of one's own social savviness (i.e., the extent to which "the situation makes you feel as though others are not as socially aware as you are"; Escoe et al., 2025, p. 670).
text.formatted: In this account, sharing cringe content is motivated by downward social comparison that boosts perceptions of one's own social savviness (i.e., the extent to which "the situation makes you feel as though others are not as socially aware as you are"; <ref type="bibr">Escoe et al., 2025, p. 670</ref>).

text.text: Escoe's account implies that, because cringe arises when observers fail to excuse the actor's behavior, it should be accompanied by less empathy than empathetic embarrassment.
Consequently, we measured whether participants experienced differences in empathy and sympathy toward the transgressor between cringe-inducing and vicariously embarrassing scenarios.

Additionally, prior work shows that observers' responses depend on why a norm was violated: vicarious embarrassment and compassion tend to be weaker when the violation is intentional, and arousal is stronger when the actor is aware of the violation (Krach et al., 2011; Müller-Pinzler et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Additionally, prior work shows that observers' responses depend on why a norm was violated: vicarious embarrassment and compassion tend to be weaker when the violation is intentional, and arousal is stronger when the actor is aware of the violation <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Krach et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Müller-Pinzler et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: However, this work did not distinguish vicarious embarrassment from cringe, and many of its stimuli resemble what people colloquially call cringe (e.g., "you are in a café: the person next to you is listening to music and singing along loudly"; Müller-Pinzler et al., 2012, p. 76), raising the possibility that intent is precisely what separates cringe from vicarious embarrassment.
text.formatted: However, this work did not distinguish vicarious embarrassment from cringe, and many of its stimuli resemble what people colloquially call cringe (e.g., "you are in a café: the person next to you is listening to music and singing along loudly"; <ref type="bibr">Müller-Pinzler et al., 2012, p. 76)</ref>, raising the possibility that intent is precisely what separates cringe from vicarious embarrassment.

text.text: Because intentional violations are treated as diagnostic of an actor's character in a way that accidental ones are not (Epley & Waytz, 2010; Reeder, 2009), cringe should differentially shape attitudes and behavior toward the transgressor as compared to vicarious embarrassment.
text.formatted: Because intentional violations are treated as diagnostic of an actor's character in a way that accidental ones are not <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Epley & Waytz, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Reeder, 2009)</ref>, cringe should differentially shape attitudes and behavior toward the transgressor as compared to vicarious embarrassment.

text.text: Therefore, we measured participants' judgments of the transgressor's actions as intentional as well as their prosocial motivation to help them, their desire to distance themselves from the transgressor, and their willingness to endorse socially sanctioning them.
Across five studies (three preregistered) we investigated the characteristics and components of trait and state cringe.
We had three main aims in the present work.

First, if cringe is a genuine affective state with a dispositional component, we should be able to measure individual differences in it, and those differences should predict how people actually respond to cringe-inducing content.

To do this, we developed and validated a novel scale to measure individual differences in trait cringe sensitivity (henceforth Cringe Scale) and tested whether it predicts perceptions of situations as cringe-inducing, influenced behavioral outcomes, and assessed its discriminant and criterion validity (Studies 1-3).

Second, to determine whether cringe is a distinct variety of vicarious embarrassment that differs in its effect on social attitudes and behavior, we tested whether cringe is associated with dissociable effects on social evaluation, empathic responses, behavioral outcomes, and attitudes on punishment and social sanctioning as compared to vicarious embarrassment (Studies 3-5).

Additionally, to support our hypothesis that attributed intent is what separates cringe from vicarious embarrassment, we tested whether cringe transgressions were perceived as more intentional than vicariously embarrassing transgressions and directly manipulated transgressor intent (Studies 4-5).
Third, if cringe functions to motivate norm-enforcement and acts as a social signal, it should be tied to sanctioning and should be stronger when the transgression is public.

We test this by investigating whether cringe is more strongly associated with endorsement of punishment and social sanctioning (e.g., gossip) than vicarious embarrassment, and by manipulating whether hypothetical transgressions occur in public or private to determine how reputation salience influences cringe perceptions (Studies 5).

If the Cringe Scale reliably captures trait cringe, discriminates it from trait vicarious embarrassment, and predicts cringe perceptions and behavioral outcomes, this would provide evidence that cringe sensitivity is a measurable individual difference that shapes how people respond to cringe-inducing situations that is conceptually distinct from vicarious embarrassment at the trait level.

Additionally, if cringe is elicited more strongly than vicarious embarrassment by intentional and public transgressions, and is accompanied by distinct inferences and behavioral attitudes towards the transgressor, this would indicate that cringe is a distinct variety of vicarious embarrassment with its own elicitors and social functions.

Importantly, these possibilities are not mutually exclusive: cringe may overlap substantially with vicarious embarrassment at the trait level while still differing in its situational elicitors and social-cognitive consequences.
Studies 1-3 developed and validated the Cringe Scale.
Study 1 generated candidate items and conducted an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) to determine the factor structure and loadings.
Study 2 confirmed this structure with confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) in a representative sample from the US and tested whether it predicted cringe perceptions.

Study 3 replicated the CFA, assessed the scale's discriminant validity from trait vicarious embarrassment, and tested whether it predicted cringe perceptions and behavioral outcomes beyond vicarious embarrassment.

Studies 4 and 5 examined the appraisals and social inferences that functionally distinguish cringe from vicarious embarrassment, with Study 5 manipulating the transgressor's intent and whether the transgression occurred in public or private.

We sampled N = 193 participants (64.8% female), aged 18-75 (MAge = 38.2) from Prolific.
Participants were compensated $1.40 for participating in a 7-min survey.

We conducted an a priori power calculation using the semPower package (Moshagen & Bader, 2024) in R to determine the number of participants needed to reject a model based on a root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) of 0.05, 169 degrees of freedom, 90% power, and an alpha of 0.05 (Jobst et al., 2023).

text.text: The analysis suggested a minimum sample of 148 observations.
We consequently oversampled to account for potential attrition due to failed attention checks or incomplete submissions.
Participants provided informed consent and were given instructions for the task.

Participants then received 80 short items detailing different behaviors (e.g., "I blush when I see something awkward happening") and indicated their agreement with each on a 7-point Likert scale anchored from "1 -Completely disagree" to "7 -Completely agree".

The items were drafted by the authors based on a review of existing literature to measure the four initially hypothesized subfactors of cringe: vicarious embarrassmentfoot_1 , physiological reactivity, norm sensitivity, and fakeness-inauthenticity.

text.text: Participants answered 20 items for each domain as well as an attention check measure ("if you're paying attention, select 2").

Because we hypothesized that cringe is a variety of vicarious embarrassment elicited by distinct triggers, these domains were intended to capture both general vicarious embarrassment (vicarious embarrassment, physiological reactivity, and norm sensitivity) and sensitivity to inauthenticity, that is, effortful, insincere, image-motivated self-presentation.
We first tested for the suitability of factor analysis using Bartlett's test of sphericity and the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin criterion.
To determine the number of factors to extract, we examined eigenvalues from principal axis factoring alongside a scree plot.
We then conducted an exploratory factor analysis on the 80-items using maximum likelihood estimation with Promax rotation, as we expected the factors to be correlated.
Relatedly, we computed the total variance explained by the factors by summing item communalities divided by the number of total items (Revelle, 2026).
text.formatted: Relatedly, we computed the total variance explained by the factors by summing item communalities divided by the number of total items <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Revelle, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: After extraction and rotation, items were evaluated based on statistical and conceptual criteria.
We used a factor loading cutoff of 0.6, indicating a very strong loading to the latent factor, to select the final scale items.

Bartlett's test of sphericity was significant (χ²(3160) = 11034.65, p < .001) and the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin criterion of sampling adequacy was .914, confirming the suitability of the data for factor analysis.
text.formatted: Bartlett's test of sphericity was significant (χ²(3160) = 11034.65, p < .001) and the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin criterion of sampling adequacy was .914, confirming the suitability of the data for factor analysis.

text.text: An examination of the eigenvalues and scree plot suggested a two-factor structure: the scree plot revealed a distinct flattening after the second factor and the two factors had eigenvalues of 25.77 and 4.56 from principal axis factoring.
After Promax rotation, the two factors explained 25% and 12% of the variance, respectively, and were moderately correlated (r = .58).
Together, the two factors explained 38% of the variance in the data.
Excluding item factor loadings below 0.6 resulted in 37 items.
To avoid redundancy, we removed items that shared similar wording, and to ensure conceptual breadth, selected the remaining items that best captured the intended construct domains.

This resulted in 20 final scale items: 12 items capturing the first latent factor of Vicarious Social Anxiety (and which included three of our initially hypothesized domains: vicarious embarrassment, involuntary physiological reactivity, and norm sensitivity), and 8 items capturing the second latent factor of Inauthenticity (capturing our fourth hypothesized subcomponent of cringe).

text.text: The results of the exploratory factor analysis from Study 1 indicated a two-factor model was most appropriate for capturing individual variability in the Cringe Scale items.
Vicarious embarrassment, physiological reactivity, and norm sensitivity loaded onto a single factor, Vicarious Social Anxiety, whereas inauthenticity emerged as a separate factor.

We retained both factors because they map onto our account of cringe: Vicarious Social Anxiety captures the vicarious embarrassment that cringe shares with related emotions, whereas Inauthenticity captures sensitivity to the intentional, image-motivated transgressions we hypothesized to be specific to cringe.
In the next study, we test this model using confirmatory factor analysis with a new sample.
The results of Study 1 allowed us to specify our cringe sensitivity model.
In Study 2, we tested this model using confirmatory factor analysis with a new, representative sample of US participants.
We also tested for predictive validity of our scale by examining whether individual differences in cringe sensitivity would predict state perceptions of cringe across a series of different stimuli.

text.text: After answering the Cringe Scale items, participants were randomly assigned between-subjects to a cringe or neutral scenario condition in which they received 10 short scenarios, 4 vignettes, and 4 short (around 1 minute) videos corresponding to their experimental condition.
Participants rated their perceptions of cringe for each stimulus on a 100-point sliding scale anchored from "0 -Not cringe at all" to "100 -Extremely cringe".
Both the order of the individual stimuli and of the three stimuli blocks was randomized across participants.
Participants then answered several basic demographic questions (age, sex, race, education level, etc.), including items noting whether they had seen the video stimuli previously.

We estimated a preregistered two-factor latent model using confirmatory factor analysis with maximum likelihood in which items 1-12 would load onto factor one-Vicarious Social Anxiety-and that items 13-20 would load onto factor two-Inauthenticity.
We then conducted a series of planned linear regression models.

To determine whether the cringe condition predicted cringe perceptions, we ran a multilevel regression model predicting cringe perceptions by condition (neutral, cringe), controlling for the random effect of participant ID.

To test whether individual differences in cringe sensitivity influence perceptions of a situation as cringeworthy, we ran a multilevel regression model predicting cringe perceptions by average Cringe Scale score across the 20-items.

To determine whether the type of stimuli influenced cringe perceptions, we ran two exploratory multilevel regression models with cringe perceptions as the response term, one including the interaction of scenario condition and stimuli modality as a predictor, and another with the interaction of Cringe Scale score and stimuli modality as a predictor (see Table S10 in the supplement).

text.text: We also conducted three exploratory multilevel regression models examining the effect of scenario condition on cringe perceptions for each stimuli type separately (short scenarios, long vignettes, videos).
Lastly, we ran two exploratory multilevel regression models predicting cringe perceptions by average Cringe Scale score.
The first was identical to the model described above but only included data from the cringe condition, and the second model controlled for the effect of scenario condition.

text.text: Study 2's findings provided confirmatory evidence in support of the Cringe Scale's twofactor structure.
More generally, these findings suggest that sensitivity to cringe varies systematically across individuals and can be measured using an individual-differences scale.

Moreover, our finding that the Cringe Scale predicted perceptions of a situation as cringeworthy provides evidence of predictive validity for our scale by demonstrating that individual differences in cringe sensitivity are associated with different social perceptions of stimuli as cringe inducing.
In Study 3, we further validated the Cringe Scale and tested it's discriminant validity.

Namely, we sought to demonstrate that our scale 1) specifically captures cringe as opposed to vicarious embarrassment, and 2) offers unique predictive validity of cringe perceptions and behavioral outcomes above and beyond vicarious embarrassment.

Additionally, we investigated the effects of cringe on consumer, public health, and charity messaging, specifically testing whether higher trait cringe was associated with reduced donations and behavioral intentions in response to cringe-inducing videos.
We sampled N = 307 participants (51.8% female), aged 19-72 (MAge = 38.74) from Prolific in a preregistered study: https://osf.io/2q73k/overview?view_only=4ecf65adc28d47ac9ea670175c3bc12b.

text.text: Participants were compensated $2.50 for participating in a 15-min survey.
We initially recruited 328 participants, but 21 were excluded for failing our inclusion criteria.
We determined our sample size based on our previous studies and established convention with online psychometric work (Loustau et al., 2025; Uysal et al., 2014).

text.text: Our goal in Study 3 was to replicate the CFA model findings from the previous study and begin to tease apart cringe from vicarious embarrassment.
To that end, participants completed our 20-item Cringe Scale from Study 2 as well as the 8-item Vicarious Embarrassment scale (VES; Uysal et al., 2014), which they received in a random order.
text.formatted: To that end, participants completed our 20-item Cringe Scale from Study 2 as well as the 8-item Vicarious Embarrassment scale (VES; <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Uysal et al., 2014)</ref>, which they received in a random order.

text.text: Participants then answered five short cringe scenarios and three cringe vignettes from the previous study presented in a random order (see Study 3 -Supplementary Materials for stimuli).
Participants were then randomly assigned to either a cringe or neutral emotion condition between-subjects and saw five videos corresponding to their assigned condition in a fixed order.

They received two videos from nonprofits-the American Red Cross and American Cancer Society-and three videos from other organizations-an Ad Council message on mental health, a McDonald's ad, and the Truth Initiative anti-vaping ad-in that order.
Participants completed an incentivized donation task (i.e., a dictator game with the nonprofit as the recipient) after watching each of the nonprofit videos.
Specifically, participants received $1 and could divide it between themselves and the nonprofit however they wished in increments of 1 cent.

After making their two donation decisions, participants received the other three videos-for each, they were asked to report their intentions of engaging in the target behavior in the video (e.g., "are you more or less likely to purchase food from McDonald's after watching this video"; see Study 3 -Method in the supplement for all intent measures) on a 100-point sliding scale anchored from "0 -Much less likely" to "100 -Much more likely", with a midpoint of "50 -Neither less nor more likely".
For the final video from the Truth Initiative's anti-vaping campaign, we also measured whether participants chose to click a provided link to visit the organization's donation page.
Participants then reported whether they had seen the videos before and, as a manipulation check, reported their cringe perceptions of each video.

To control for factors that might influence donation decisions and behavioral intentions, participants answered a series of questions assessing how often they engage in the target behavior associated with each video (e.g., for the Ad Council video on mental health: "how often do you discuss mental health with family members or friends").

Lastly, participants answered an item assessing how much time they spend on various social media platforms, a one-item cringe sensitivity measure (i.e., "on a scale of 1 -100, how sensitive are you to cringey situations"), as well as a number of demographic questions.
See Study 3 -Results in the supplement for the results of the social media and cringe sensitivity analyses.
We first replicated our confirmatory factor analysis with a new sample to provide additional evidence of our scale's model fit and internal reliability.
To test for discriminant validity between the Cringe Scale and the VES, we used confirmatory factor analysis to compare two models, an unconstrained and a constrained model.

The latent factors of Cringe and Vicarious embarrassment were allowed to freely covary with one another in the unconstrained model, whereas the latent correlations were fixed to 0.85 in the constrained model, following the approach of Panzeri et al. (2024).

(2024)</ref>.

text.text: If the unconstrained model demonstrated a latent correlation < 0.85, and had a better model fit than the constrained model-i.e., the difference in CFI between the models is greater than 0.002, and the χ2 difference between the two models is statistically significant (where α = 0.05)-we interpreted this as evidence of discriminant validity.

text.text: In order to examine the relationship of trait cringe and vicarious embarrassment on cringe perceptions and behavior, we fit a series of preregistered regression models.
All multilevel regression models included participant ID as a random intercept.

Specifically, to determine whether the Cringe Scale uniquely predicts cringe perceptions above and beyond the VES, we tested and compared two multilevel regression models-the first predicting cringe perceptions by scores on the vicarious embarrassment scale (Uysal et al., 2014), and the second predicting cringe perceptions by both VES score and Cringe Scale score.

text.text: We then compared these nested models using a likelihood ratio test to determine whether the model with trait cringe score explains significantly more variance than the model solely including vicarious embarrassment.

To further probe the predictive and discriminant validity of the Cringe Scale, we ran a series of exploratory models predicting cringe perceptions by the VES and each of the Cringe Scale's two latent factors (factor 1: Vicarious Social Anxiety and factor 2: Inauthenticity) and compared each to a nested model including only the VES.

Finally, to determine whether the Cringe Scale and VES differed in their ability to predict cringe perceptions, we assessed whether there was a statistically significant difference in the coefficients (α = 0.05) using the approach of Zee (2019).

text.text: Specifically, we compared regression coefficients using seemingly unrelated regression (SUR) and tested for differences between coefficients using Theil's F test.

We then conducted several regression models predicting behavioral outcomes by Cringe Scale score-we report the results of two models here: the first including incentivized donation decisions as the outcome variable, and the second including behavioral intentions.
We report the models individually examining each specific behavioral outcome in the supplement (see Study 3 -Results in the supplement).

To determine whether scenario condition predicted behavioral outcomes, we conducted a series of identical regression models but including scenario condition (neutral, cringe) as the predictor rather than Cringe Scale score.

We report the results of the two combined multilevel regression models here (one looking at incentivized donations, the other looking at behavioral intentions) and report the models for each individual behavioral outcome in the supplement.

Next, to determine whether the Cringe Scale predicts behavioral outcomes above and beyond the VES, we compared a multilevel regression model including both Cringe Scale and VES scores as predictors to a nested model including only the VES using a likelihood ratio test, both for overall behavioral outcomes and separately for behavioral intentions and donation decisions.

As with cringe perceptions, we also ran exploratory models predicting behavioral outcomes by the VES and each of the Cringe Scale's two latent factors, comparing each to a nested model including only the VES.
All multilevel models were refit with an additional random intercept for stimulus identity; all converged and no conclusions changed.

Estimates for trait cringe and the VES were virtually identical, and the (non-significant) effects of video condition had larger standard errors because each condition used a different set of five videos.
We report the participant random-intercept models in keeping with our preregistration.

To more clearly test for discriminant validity, we ran a series of exploratory analyses duplicating the CFA and Cringe Scale-VES regression models excluding the two shared items with the VES-we report those results in the supplement; the regression results were consistent with our preregistered models, and the discriminant validity results are summarized below.

Lastly, since the Cringe Scale and VES were highly correlated, we also tested for potential multicollinearity in regression models where both scale scores and their factors were entered as predictors by computing variance inflation factors (VIFs; James et al., 2021).

The latent correlation between Vicarious Social Anxiety and VES was r = 0.919 (95% CI: 0.895, 0.943) and the latent correlation between Inauthenticity and VES was r = 0.756 (95% CI: 0.7, 0.813).
The association between the two Cringe Scale latent factors was high and significant, r = 0.87 (p < .001).

For Vicarious Social Anxiety, the latent correlation exceeded .85 (r = .92, 95% CI [.90, .94]).

For Inauthenticity, the latent correlation was below .85 (r = .76, 95% CI [.70, .81]) and constraining it significantly worsened fit (Δχ²(1) = 15.19, p < .001), but the decrease in CFI (.0019) fell just short of the .002 criterion.

text.text: This suggests that the second Cringe Scale factor-Inauthenticity-specifically provides additional predictive validity of cringe perceptions over the VES.

However, when testing whether the Cringe Scale and VES differed in their ability to predict cringe assessments by comparing regression coefficients using seemingly unrelated regression (SUR), we found that a Theil's F test indicated no significant difference between the coefficients (F(1, 590) = 0.10, p = .75), suggesting both scales have equivalent predictive validity for cringe assessments.

The Cringe Scale significantly predicted behavioral outcomes (B = 6.15, SE = 0.94, p < .001), including both behavioral intentions (B = 6.80, SE = 0.99, p < .001) and donation decisions (B = 5.17, SE = 1.46, p < .001), but in the opposite direction of what was predicted; higher trait cringe was positively, rather than negatively, associated with behavioral outcomes.

text.text: In an exploratory model, this association did not differ by video condition (Cringe Scale × condition: B = -0.21, SE = 1.90, p = .91), indicating that higher trait cringe was associated with greater donations and intentions regardless of whether participants viewed cringe-inducing or neutral videos.

Additionally, there was no effect of emotion condition on overall behavioral outcomes (B = -1.01, SE = 2.55, p = .69), including for behavioral intentions (B = -3.18, SE = 2.68, p = .24), donations (B = 2.25, SE = 3.76, p = .55) and clicking the Truth Initiative donation link (B = 0.29, SE = 0.37, p = .43).

The only stimuli for which we observed an effect of emotion condition was for the behavioral intentions to the Ad Council videos on mental health (B = -9.31, SE = 3.19, p = .004), where intentions to discuss mental health with family and friends were lower in the cringe than neutral video.

When comparing the model including both cringe and VES as predictors of behavioral outcomes to a nested model only including the VES, we found that, in contrast to our prediction, the model with cringe did not explain significantly more variance than the model without (LRT χ² (1) = 1.61, p = .21).
This held true when separately examining behavioral intentions (LRT χ² (1) = 1.53, p = .22) and donation decisions (LRT χ² (1) = 0.63, p = .43).

However, when breaking up the Cringe Scale by its two latent factors, we found that the model including Vicarious Social Anxiety (B = 3.54, SE = 1.73, p = .04) and VES (B = 2.83, SE = 1.65, p = .09), explained significantly more variance in behavioral outcomes than a model with just VES (LRT χ² (1) = 4.20, p = .04), suggesting that the first factor of the Cringe Scale offers unique predictive validity over and above the VES.

Because the Vicarious Social Anxiety factor and the VES were highly correlated, multicollinearity was higher in this model (VIF = 4.1 for each predictor) than in the two-factor Cringe Scale models (VIF = 3.4), though still below the conventional cutoff of 5 indicating moderate multicollinearity (James et al., 2021).
